about: THE OUTCOME WEB, version 1 (04 SYSTEM SPECS part 5; research in docs/research/outcome-web-2026-09-28.md). Each link: how a cause measure moves an outcome measure. evidence says how well the link is established (researched, provisional, contested, about-zero, to-confirm). size is the proportional change in the outcome per unit of the cause (see per); null means the size is set when both measures exist in the world. about-zero links are zero on purpose and tested. Sources are for developers only and never appear on a player screen. A cause named law:<qualified question key> is what the law in force says on a policy question (governing/law-in-force.ts): 1 when it says yes, 0 when it says no, and unrecorded where no law has answered it. A law cause is measured from the place's law on the calibration date (calibratedAt): its base data already includes the law in force then, so only a change from it moves the outcome. law:us-federal-positions:<key> is a question only Congress answers. A link's size is a baseline, not a literal number: each world draws the size for each place from the link's range (the spread the research reports), or from a default spread by evidence (researched 25% either way, provisional 50%, contested from none to twice the size). About-zero links stay at zero.

links.per: percentage point of residents receiving SNAP that a law or other cause moved
links.anchor: SNAP cuts a household's chance of food insecurity about 30%. 51.1% of households that received SNAP in 2024 were food insecure, so without it about 73% would be: 21.9 points more for each household that loses SNAP. SNAP households average 1.9 people and all households 2.5, so a point of residents is 1.3% of households, and food insecurity rises 0.29 points, 2.1% of the 13.7% national rate. The low end reads the 30% against the rate with SNAP (15.3 points); the high end is a quarter above the center. Only the part of SNAP receipt that a law or other cause moved counts: the share's own drift stands for changes in need, which move food insecurity the other way.
links.source: Ratcliffe, McKernan and Zhang 2011, American Journal of Agricultural Economics 93(4); USDA ERS, Household Food Security in the United States in 2024 (ERR-358), table 8; USDA FNS, Characteristics of SNAP Households: Fiscal Year 2023; Census Bureau, America's Families and Living Arrangements: 2024

links.per: law in force: about +1 point on a turnout near 66% of eligible voters
links.anchor: AVR raises registration a lot; the new registrants vote less often than others, but enough of them vote to raise the eligible turnout rate, and the effect builds the longer AVR is in place. Front-end registration (at the agency visit) raised turnout 1.1 points and back-end registration (a notice after the visit) 3.3 points, as Data for Progress quotes the paper; the front-end size is used, with the back-end one as the top of the range. For people whose registration AVR updated when they moved, turnout rose 5.8 points (Orange County, California), which bounds it from above.
links.source: McGhee, Hill and Romero 2021, The Registration and Turnout Effects of Automatic Voter Registration (SSRN 3933442); Kim 2021, APSA preprint (doi 10.33774/apsa-2021-3wzbh)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0); zero where the place already restores the vote by the end of a sentence
links.group: people barred from voting after their sentence
links.anchor: Restoring the vote at the end of a sentence adds people to the voting-eligible population who vote less than others, so the eligible turnout rate falls while ballots rise. Each place's size is (1 + s x t / T) / (1 + s) - 1: s is its share of the voting-eligible population barred after their sentence, t = 0.14 the turnout of restored people (0.12 to 0.22 for the range) and T its 2024 turnout. In Tennessee the rate falls about 4% while ballots rise about 0.8 points of the old eligible population. The places that already restore by the end of a sentence (the rest of the states, D.C., the territories, and Arkansas, where Locked Out 2024 counts no one barred after the sentence, as Research 3 read it) have no one for the law to restore.
links.source: The Sentencing Project, Locked Out 2024 (post-sentence shares by state); Meredith and Morse, Florida restorations 2007 to 2011 (12 to 16% voted); Burch 2011 (about 22%); University of Florida Election Lab 2024 VEP turnout. Prohibiting payday loans goes with a 35% decline in their use (Urban Institute working paper, read); the published version reports 32%. A state rate cap of 36% APR ends storefront payday lending as a prohibition does. Cross-state survey evidence, not a trial. Read on the count of consumer lenders, a stand-in for use. links.source: Dragone, Prarolo, Vanin and Zanella 2019, Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization 159

links.anchor: At today's incarceration levels, longer or mandatory sentences have little effect on crime
links.source: Roodman 2017, The Impacts of Incarceration on Crime (Open Philanthropy)

links.anchor: Five to nine years after enactment, states with stringent renewable standards cut power-plant sulfur dioxide about 58% and nitrogen oxides about 34%; power plants are a small share of today's fine particles
links.source: Ji, Li, Lee, Luke and Mavrothalassitis 2024, working paper, Cleaner Bills, Cleaner Air

links.anchor: California's cap-and-trade lowered fine-particle emissions at regulated plants 3 to 9% a year from 2012 to 2017; the statewide change in the air is far smaller
links.source: Hernandez-Cortes and Meng 2023, Journal of Public Economics 217

links.per: law in force (a two-year rise in the full retirement age, 67 to 69)
links.anchor: A one-year rise cuts benefits 6.7% at any claiming age (5/9 of 1% a month); elderly poverty moves about one for one with benefits; people 65 and older were 6.1 million of the 35.9 million poor people in 2024 (17.0%), so each year of rise raises the poverty rate about 1.1% of itself
links.source: Engelhardt and Gruber 2004 (NBER w10466); 20 CFR 404.410; Census P60-287 (2025)

links.anchor: Across all 50 states and D.C., 1990 to 2014, undocumented immigration did not increase violent crime; the relationship was generally negative and not always significant
links.source: Light and Miller 2018 (Criminology); Ousey and Kubrin 2018 (Annual Review of Criminology)

links.anchor: Drug offenders released early under the 2014 retroactive cut reoffended no more than those who served full terms (27.9% vs 30.5% in three years); federal prisoners are a small share of all prisoners
links.source: U.S. Sentencing Commission 2020 (Drugs Minus Two recidivism); BJS Prisoners in 2023

links.anchor: Chicago's 1997 voucher lottery (82,607 applicants), children tracked 14 years: effects on schooling mostly statistically insignificant
links.source: Jacob, Kapustin and Ludwig 2015 (QJE; NBER w20164)

links.anchor: Same lottery: effects on arrests mostly statistically insignificant
links.source: Jacob, Kapustin and Ludwig 2015 (QJE; NBER w20164)

links.anchor: The official poverty measure uses money income before taxes, and the top rate reaches no one near the line
links.source: U.S. Census Bureau, How the Census Bureau measures poverty

links.anchor: Debt relief is not money income, which is what the official poverty measure counts
links.source: U.S. Census Bureau, How the Census Bureau measures poverty

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Removing the grocery tax cuts food insecurity 3.2% among households under $30,000, where most food-insecure households are, so about 2% statewide; only states that taxed groceries in 2024 change
links.source: Zheng, Zhao, Buck, Burney, Kaiser and Wilson 2021, Food Policy 101

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Naloxone access laws: opioid deaths 9 to 11% lower in one study, no net drop in another; opioids are most, not all, overdose deaths
links.source: Rees, Sabia, Argys, Latshaw and Dave 2019, Journal of Law and Economics 62(1); Doleac and Mukherjee 2022, Journal of Law and Economics 65(2)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Men schooled under teacher duty-to-bargain laws earn 3.9% less as adults; only exposed cohorts, and only men, so a small statewide share, arriving as they reach working age
links.source: Lovenheim and Willen 2019, AEJ: Economic Policy 11(3)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Library building investment raised children's reading 0.01 to 0.04 standard deviations, about 3% more at proficient; an operating floor is taken as a third of that
links.source: Gilpin, Karger and Nencka 2024, AEJ: Economic Policy

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: State bans on municipal broadband cut access about 4.5% from 2012 to 2018; that measured availability, and subscriptions move less

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: 12.7% of childhood asthma is attributed to gas stoves, from a meta-analysis of associations; a ban reaches only new buildings, so a small part of that over a decade
links.source: Gruenwald, Seals, Knibbs and Hosgood 2022, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 20(1)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Price changes at public colleges did not move degree attainment; spending did

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Taxes move few people: even millionaires rarely leave high-tax states
links.source: Young, Varner, Lurie and Prisinzano 2016, American Sociological Review

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Taxes move few people: even millionaires rarely leave high-tax states
links.source: Young, Varner, Lurie and Prisinzano 2016, American Sociological Review

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in basis points
links.anchor: States with strict anti-deficit rules paid 15 to 20 basis points less than states with lax rules on general-obligation bonds, 1973 to 1996; a statute moves a state partway, so 8
links.source: Poterba and Rueben 1999, State Fiscal Institutions and the U.S. Municipal Bond Market (NBER w6237)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in basis points
links.anchor: PLACEHOLDER (research: pension-funding-borrowing-cost-size): spreads rose 7 to 15 basis points for each 10% of revenue lost in pension funds, in states in the lower half of credit quality; paying the full contribution heads off part of that. The size is a provisional range, drawn per world (Claude CTO, September 28, 2026)
links.source: Novy-Marx and Rauh 2012, AEJ: Economic Policy 4(2)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0), in basis points
links.anchor: PLACEHOLDER (research: reserve-balance-borrowing-cost-size): rainy-day funds raise ratings and lower yields, but no study gives basis points per law; the size is a provisional range, drawn per world (Claude CTO, September 28, 2026)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Transit ridership's elasticity with respect to fares is -0.2 to -0.5 in the first year. A fare falling to zero is read on the semi-log curve the paper recommends for fares near zero, where ridership rises by e to the elasticity: 22% to 65%, 42% at the middle of the range. Long-run elasticities of -0.6 to -0.9 would give more, so this is the first year's effect, held.
links.source: Litman 2025, Transit Price Elasticities and Cross-Elasticities, Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Table 15 and page 9

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Legal adult sales went with 20 to 35% fewer opioid deaths where stores opened, which is 15 to 27% of all overdose deaths at opioids' 76% share (2022). A later check found that result fragile and stores going with more opioid deaths, so the evidence runs both ways and the middle is a small fall. The lag is the months from the law taking effect to the first store opening, averaged over six states: Colorado 13, Washington 19, Michigan 12, Illinois 0, New York 21, Missouri 2 (ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: 11)
links.source: Chan, Burkhardt and Flyr 2020, Economic Inquiry 58(2); Mathur and Ruhm 2023, Journal of Health Economics 88; CDC WONDER 2022 overdose deaths by drug

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: State privacy laws bind only large data holders: the common model reaches a business handling data on 100,000 of the state's consumers, and California's also one with $25 million in revenue. The cost falls on data firms and app makers, which lost investment and apps under Europe's rule, too small a share of a state's workers to move its median earnings
links.source: Va. Code 59.1-576; Cal. Civ. Code 1798.140(d); Jia, Jin and Wagman 2021, Marketing Science 40(4); Janssen, Kesler, Kummer and Waldfogel 2022, NBER Working Paper 30028

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Courts blocked most state laws requiring platforms to check ages before they took effect (Arkansas, Ohio, Utah, California, Texas, Maryland), and no study has measured an effect on students. Facebook's arrival at colleges hurt students' mental health and schoolwork, but an age check on a platform teenagers already use is not the reverse of its arrival
links.source: NetChoice v. Griffin, W.D. Ark. 2025; Braghieri, Levy and Makarin 2022, American Economic Review 112(11)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Leaving the choice to local boards changes which titles stay on the shelf: challenges reached 4,240 titles nationwide in 2023, a small share of any library's collection, and no study links removals to reading scores. What moves reading is money for the library itself, a different question
links.source: American Library Association, Office for Intellectual Freedom, 2023 book challenge data; Gilpin, Karger and Nencka 2024, AEJ: Economic Policy

links.per: ordinance in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: State employment protections raised gay men's wages 2.7% and lowered lesbian women's employment, too small a group to move poverty; a city's ordinance reaches fewer people still

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Where federal law let highway money go to transit (1992 to 2006), states spent about 3% of the whole federal-aid highway program on transit, 13% of the flexible part; California put nearly 40% of its flexible money there, and 19 states less than 2%. The same 3% of a state's own highway spending (Census Bureau, 2022: $128.0 billion) is 5.9% of what transit agencies spend to run service (FTA National Transit Database, 2024: $65.6 billion), so service rises about 6% at the average cost per mile. The spread takes 2% to 40% of the flexible part. The lag is a budget cycle and the buses it buys, the most common use GAO found.
links.source: GAO-07-772, Highway and Transit Investments: Flexible Funding Supports State and Local Transportation Priorities (2007); Census Bureau, 2022 Census of Governments: Finance, Table 1 (state highways); FTA National Transit Database 2024 (data.transportation.gov ekg5-frzt, total operating expenses)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Across 269 counties in six Mid-Atlantic states over 50 years, a state or local program that buys farmland development rights cut the county's rate of farmland loss by 40% to 55%. The size is the middle of that range, 47%, and the spread is the paper's own. The lag is one Census of Agriculture period, the step at which the loss was measured, since a program needs years of purchases before its easements hold back development.
links.source: Liu and Lynch 2011, Do Agricultural Land Preservation Programs Reduce Farmland Loss? Evidence from a Propensity Score Matching Estimator, Land Economics 87(2): 183-201; its 40% to 55% as reported in USDA Economic Research Service, Additionality in U.S. Agricultural Conservation and Regulatory Offset Programs, ERR-170 (2014)

links.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
links.anchor: Kansas's first Local Enhanced Management Area (Sheridan 6, 2013 to 2017), where irrigators pumped under capped five-year allocations (55 inches of water over five years), cut pumping 31% against a modeled business-as-usual over its first five years (95% interval 21% to 40%). A state law that meters and limits large withdrawals is read as putting such a cap on irrigation pumping; where the cap binds less than it did there, the cut is smaller, so the evidence is provisional. The spread is the paper's interval. The lag is one year, the next irrigation season.
links.source: Deines, Kendall, Butler and Hyndman 2019, Quantifying irrigation adaptation strategies in response to stakeholder-driven groundwater management in the US High Plains Aquifer, Environmental Research Letters 14: 044014 (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aafe39)
